subject: Anthropic's 1.7 GW of turbines, and Ontario's bill
bodyMarkdown:
The Financial Times reported yesterday that Samsung SDS is in early talks with Anthropic and OpenAI about hosting them as data centre tenants, with no terms and no capacity disclosed. I am leading with a thin story because of what it sits on top of, which is a stretch of weeks in which the AI labs stopped treating electricity as somebody else's problem.

## The lab that bought 1.7 gigawatts of generators

The Financial Times reported on November 8 that Anthropic agreed in late September to pay around $3.4 billion for commitments covering 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty gas-fired generators. The seller was OnePWR Solutions, a San Antonio developer that had ordered the machines from Caterpillar roughly two years ago and needed financing to take delivery. Anthropic took over those orders and the installation capability without buying the company. Bloomberg picked the story up the same day, and Reuters said it could not immediately verify it. Anthropic and OnePWR both declined to comment, so hold the number loosely. The arithmetic is still worth doing. That works out to roughly $2,000 per kilowatt of generation, bought as equipment rather than as a power contract. That is what it looks like when a company decides the grid will not get there in time.

## Behind the meter, and why that phrase matters

Buying turbines instead of signing a power purchase agreement points at going **behind the meter**, which means generating electricity on your own site so it never travels over the public system or lands on anyone else's bill. That is the tidiest version of this build for everyone standing outside it. OpenAI moved the same direction earlier this month, saying it will stop using nondisclosure agreements when it negotiates data centre projects and will make sure residents do not pay for the power those projects consume, which Bloomberg reported on November 5. Then comes yesterday's Samsung SDS item, which is the opposite trade. Renting space in Korea means somebody else owns the interconnection, the permits and the risk. The labs look like they are running both plays at once, owning generation where they can and renting shells where they cannot.

## Ontario already picked a side

Which brings this to my hydro bill. The IESO's 2026 Annual Planning Outlook forecasts Ontario electricity demand growing 65 per cent by 2050, with data centres climbing from 4.5 terawatt hours in 2027 to 22.6 by 2050, and the operator is tracking roughly 7,000 megawatts of data centre connection requests, about double its March figure. Ontario's answer landed in August. BNN Bloomberg reported on August 13 that new data centres will pay all their energy costs and get no cash incentives, with a proposed rate class for anything above one megawatt priced above the existing industrial rate. I think that is the right call, and I think it will get tested. A province charging full freight for power competes against American states that do not, and against labs that have shown they will just buy their own turbines.

## The takeaway

If you pay an Ontario hydro bill, follow the consultation on that new data centre rate class, because the gap between what those customers pay and what the system costs to expand is what eventually reaches you. Treat the Anthropic generator figure as a single-source report until the company confirms it, given that Reuters would not stand behind it. Watch whether other labs start buying generation outright, since turbine orders show up years before a data centre does. And if you hold a Canadian utility or pipeline, notice that the AI build is now a direct buyer of gas equipment.
